title: Brothers on Opposite Teams at the World Cup — Who Does Mom Cheer For?
summary: What if you and your sibling both made it to the World Cup — but on different teams? That’s real life for Desire and Guela Doue. The brothers grew up in Angers, France, with a French mom and an Ivorian dad. Now Desire, 21, is a star for Paris Saint-Germain and plays for France. Guela, 23, plays for Strasbourg and chose Ivory Coast. They tell each other everything and are super close. But on June 30, they could face off in Texas if both their teams finish second in their groups. Imagine your brother trying to score against you! In a friendly match earlier this month, Ivory Coast beat France 2-1, but Desire didn’t get to play. Guela said, “It’s a shame I didn’t get to play against my brother, but I’m happy, and he isn’t too fed up.” They’re not the only ones. There are four sets of brothers at this World Cup playing for different nations. Remember the Boateng brothers? Jerome played for Germany and Kevin-Prince for Ghana — they faced each other in 2010 and 2014. Now it’s the Doues’ turn. So, who will their parents cheer for? Probably both — and hope for a tie!
why_it_matters: It shows that families can love and support each other even when they are on different sides in sports, which is like when you and a friend play on opposite teams but stay friends.

background_read: The World Cup is the most-watched soccer tournament, held every four years, and players often represent their country of birth or their parents' homelands.
Ivory Coast (a country in West Africa) has produced many talented players who also play for European clubs like Paris Saint-Germain (a top French team) and Strasbourg.
It is not unusual for brothers to end up on different national teams; the Boateng brothers—Jerome for Germany, Kevin-Prince for Ghana—faced each other at the 2010 and 2014 World Cups.
Article_Structure: WHO: Brothers Desire Doue (France) and Guela Doue (Ivory Coast).
WHAT: They could face each other in a World Cup match if their teams both finish second, continuing a rare soccer tradition.
WHERE: A possible match in Texas, USA.
WHY: They chose different national teams because of their mixed heritage, creating a special family story.

perspectives.description: They love the drama of brothers competing against each other, and it makes the World Cup more exciting and memorable.
Their parents are probably very proud of both sons, even though it can be a little awkward when one has to lose.
Some might say players should only represent one country, but the rules allow choosing a parent's homeland, and both brothers are honoring their roots.
